records.chose: Detect undeclared redundancy as ENUMERATED-DOMAIN AGREEMENT: collect every site that spells out a set of string tokens (union members, enum members, object/Record keys, switch cases, ===-comparison chains, string-literal arrays, markdown table first columns, a|b|c alternations inside string literals), then pair sites whose token sets overlap
over: Signature-shaped twin detection: two functions with the same parameter and return types

records.because: The declared parity form is agreement over an ENUMERATED DOMAIN, so the undeclared version of it must be a domain spelled twice. Type-shape twins are hopelessly common in TS ((s:string)=>string appears everywhere) and clone detection finds copy-paste, which is a maintenance smell, not a divergence risk -- neither is informative WITHOUT a prior claim about the value, which is the whole point. A duplicated token SET is: if the two sets are unequal the transcription has already drifted, which is signal with no declaration needed.

records.chose: the instrument candidate is guaranteed at the WRITE (withInstrumentCandidate in decisions.ts write()), with a deliberately narrow keyword heuristic deciding only the WORDING

add it at the render so nothing on disk is synthesised

records.because: at the write it is inside the content hash, so a re-logged conjecture still dedupes to one id, and every path in (CLI, hook, test, future tool) gets it. The heuristic's failure mode is asymmetric ON PURPOSE: a false negative prepends a redundant canonical candidate (noise, recoverable); a false positive would ship a conjecture with no instrument doubt at all (silent, and the exact failure this record exists to prevent). Demonstrated live: 'a paste/editor artifact' did NOT trip the heuristic, so the canonical line was added alongside it.

records.because: A Record<OracleVerdict,X> table CANNOT drift from its union -- tsc checks the keys. Reporting it is a false positive by construction, and this repo's own ladder says that tier belongs to the type system, not to coherence. On the first dogfood run 15 of 35 overlapping pairs were compiler-enforced: without this rule the report would have been ~40 percent noise before any ranking. It also gives the reader the tier-1 FIX for free -- annotate the literal and the finding disappears.

records.chose: dedupe on a stored `metric` label, one OPEN conjecture per label at a time — and a RESOLVED one keeps the label quiet until the value moves a further threshold-width past the value that was resolved
over: dedupe on the content-hash id (the existing mechanism) — it cannot work, because the value is IN the observation text and changes every run, so ten runs mint ten ids and ten open questions

dedupe on label forever, so a label that ever produced a conjecture never produces another — that trades the spam generator for a silence generator: the second, larger excursion is exactly the one worth asking about
dedupe on a time window (one conjecture per label per day/run) — a clock is not the identity of a question, and it re-opens on a schedule rather than on new evidence
records.because: the identity of the QUESTION is 'why is <label> outside its band', which is stable across runs while the number is not. So the dedupe key must be the label, not the measurement. The resolved-state rule falls out of the same reading: a resolution answers the excursion it was written against, so an excursion that has moved a further threshold-width beyond the resolved value is a DIFFERENT question and deserves to be asked. Requires storing `value` on the record, which the journal wanted anyway

records.chose: return-to-band NEVER auto-resolves; it prints the open conjecture's id and the exact `coherence resolved` line instead
over: auto-resolve when the metric comes back inside its band
auto-retract the conjecture on return, on the theory that the observation stopped holding
records.because: a resolution's `because` field is what the discriminating test SHOWED. A number wandering back shows nothing about the cause, so an auto-resolution would have to write a false claim ('it came back') into the one field that carries evidence. The failure is also silent and asymmetric: it deletes an entry from `decisions --open` — the single list this feature exists to populate — and deletes it precisely in the case where nobody looked. And it closes the most interesting questions preferentially: a metric that left its band and returned has usually done something stranger (a transient, an accidental revert, a non-monotonicity) than one that stayed out. Silence is the other failure, so the return IS reported — on stdout, as evidence a human may resolve WITH, never as the resolution

records.chose: an explained move (--why) is written as a conjecture PLUS its resolution — born answered — and when a conjecture is already open for that label the --why RESOLVES it
over: a plain `decision` record: it would land in Standing with an empty `over`, reporting a metric move as a settled choice
a new record kind `observation`, with its own render section
writing nothing at all when --why is present, on the grounds that the source file already holds the explanation
records.because: the journal already has exactly the shape 'a notable move, and what accounted for it': a conjecture with a resolution pointing at it. Reusing it means an explained-immediately move and an explained-three-weeks-later move render identically, which is correct — the reader cares what the answer is, not how fast it arrived. It also needs no new kind, no new render branch, and no change to resolve(). The open-conjecture case is the loop closing itself: coherence asked the question, the project filled in the `why` field its own table already has, and the next harness run carries that answer back in

records.chose: match the consuming table's `Math.abs(delta) >= threshold` byte-for-byte, float wobble included, instead of adding an epsilon or a relative tolerance
over: an epsilon around the threshold, so a move of 'exactly one band' in decimal counts as notable
a relative comparison (|delta| / |baseline|) so the bar scales with the metric
records.because: measured while writing the test: 0.15 - 0.14 is 0.00999999999999998, so a decimal move that LOOKS like exactly one band is under a 0.010 threshold and the row prints as not-moved. Any correction here would be a correction coherence applied and planetizer did not, and the two halves would then disagree exactly at the boundary — the one place a disagreement is invisible, because it is the case nobody eyeballs. Being wrong the SAME way is worth more than being right alone. The relative form is worse still: notableDelta is an ABSOLUTE physical quantity (o2's 0.01 is a tenth of the O2_ANIMAL_MIN..O2_FIRE_THRESHOLD band), and dividing it by the baseline would silently re-scale a bar the project derived from the manual. Pinned in test/observed.test.ts as a fact, not routed around

records.chose: negative controls on BOTH new behaviours: the label dedupe and the refusal to auto-resolve

records.chose: usage errors exit 2, against the brief's letter of 'exit code 0 always'
over: exit 0 unconditionally, including on --value banana or a missing --threshold, as literally specified
records.because: the brief's 'exit 0 always. This gates nothing' is about the OBSERVATION — a metric outside its band must never fail a build, and it does not: outside, inside, opened, deduped, resolved all exit 0, pinned by a CLI test. A malformed invocation is not an observation. Exiting 0 on a typo'd flag would make the harness stop asking questions silently, which is this repo's own named defect ('a command that exits 0 and does nothing, which is the defect this harness exists to hunt', cli.ts resolved branch) and the same failure as the negative control whose regex never matched. --threshold in particular has no default and must not acquire one: the bar is domain knowledge that lives on the project's side of the seam, so a missing one is a missing BAR, not a zero

records.chose: leave `observed` out of agentInstructions — the text every agent is handed at startup
over: adding a fourth verb to the startup instruction alongside decide/blocked/conjecture/retract
records.because: that string is paid for by every agent on every job, and the conjecture pass already logged an open question about whether agents reach for a verb they were not told about (d-04198572). But observed is not an agent verb: its caller is a harness with a metric table, once per row per run. An agent that needs it is an agent BUILDING the harness, and that agent is reading the README, where the division of labour now lives. records.chose: an advisory finding's identity is its SUBJECT — the addressable thing a reader would go look at — stored in a new `finding` field and namespaced by the advisory that formed it
over: hash the rendered finding text (the content hash the journal already has)
reuse observed's `metric` field with a namespaced value
key on the token sets / the claim's run count / the pair's score
records.because: the score is the most volatile thing in the redundancy report: `df` is GLOBAL, so adding a token anywhere in the tree re-ranks every pair. A key containing it opens a new question per run. Line numbers are navigation, not structure (cli.ts already normalizes them out of graph.json for exactly this reason), so the site key is file#kind:name with the line dropped. `metric` was rejected as the carrier because its docblock says it holds a tracked metric and a raise has no number — a field whose name lies is the next reader's trap.

records.chose: the volume guard is THREE layers: --raise opt-in, the advisory's own reporting floor, and a hard per-run cap that announces what it withheld
over: opt-in alone
the reporting floor alone
a cap alone
records.because: each layer fails differently and the failure modes do not overlap. Opt-in stops a pre-commit verify from silently writing to the journal (planetizer runs verify in its hook). The floor stops `redundancy --all` — which drops minScore to 0 — from raising the tail it exists to expose; raising always uses the DEFAULT floor, never --all's. The cap bounds the FIRST run on a repo with a long list, which is the case that kills the mechanism on contact. Silence about the withheld remainder was rejected outright: a truncated list that looks complete is the defect this harness hunts.

records.chose: dismissal is a new record KIND that supersedes a conjecture, ranked below retraction and below resolution
over: a flag on the resolution record (`resolved --dismiss`)
a `dismissed` list in config, keyed on the finding
deleting the conjecture line
records.because: "we answered this" and "we decided not to ask" are different facts and the render has to be able to lead with the first. A flag on a resolution would put a dismissal in the Resolved section, where a reader counts it as an answer — the same confusion `resolve()` already refuses between a conjecture and a decision. A config list would be an EDIT; the journal is append-only and a dismissal that rewrites history is indistinguishable from one that was always right. Precedence: retraction (the observation was never real) beats resolution (we know the answer) beats dismissal (we chose not to ask), because showing a dismissal for a question that has an answer on file HIDES the answer.

records.chose: the per-run cap is spent ROUND-ROBIN across advisories, not in strict priority order
over: strict priority (never-red, then warned-kind, then refutation) with the starvation made visible in the withheld line
records.because: the first dogfood run refuted the priority design on the spot: planetizer @HEAD offered 14 never-red findings and 3 warned-kind, and the withheld line read `never-red 9 · warned-kind 3` — every warned-kind question queued behind twelve others, on the one repo whose config explicitly declares that kind the suspect one. Visible starvation is still starvation. Round-robin bounds it at one round per advisory and the caller's ranking still orders within a round.

records.chose: the COMMAND registry lives in a new src/commands.ts, not in src/cli.ts beside the dispatch
over: src/cli.ts, adjacent to the if/else dispatch it describes
src/render-commands.ts, matching the render-* naming convention
records.because: cli.ts EXECUTES at import time (top-level process.argv dispatch and process.exit), so a test that imports a registry living there would run the CLI and exit(2) — the totality oracle is the whole point of the exercise and it must be able to import the source of truth. render-* was rejected because the registry and its two derived spellings are the reason the file exists; splitting them buys an import hop and nothing else.

records.chose: a registry + a totality oracle that reads the LIVE dispatch out of cli.ts's AST, with the banner and the README index derived
over: a Record<name, handler> dispatch table that deletes the correspondence outright instead of checking it
a hand-written expected-command list in the test
records.because: the handler table is the strongest form and should happen eventually, but cli.ts's dispatch is 350 lines of early exits, shared locals and per-command usage errors: rewriting it to land a documentation fix trades a checked correspondence for an unchecked rewrite. A hand-written expected list was rejected outright — it would be a FOURTH spelling of the same domain and would drift exactly like the other three. The oracle reads the AST rather than a regex because a regex also matches cmd === "x" inside a comment, and an oracle a code comment can fool is not one.

records.chose: the derived README index is a BULLET LIST, and the scaffold entry's usage reads <kind> rather than spelling its four kinds

carrying <boundary|component|invariant|parity> through from the old banner line
records.because: redundancy reads the first column of every markdown table as an enumerated domain, so a generated table hands it a fresh README-vs-dispatch pair — trading the finding this change removes for an identical one, which fixes nothing. Same reasoning one level down for the scaffold kinds: a DERIVED index propagates whatever the registry spells, and README already spelled those four in prose, so carrying them added a pair. Measured: with <kind>, redundancy goes 42 pairs to 37 with ZERO added; carrying the alternation added one new sub-floor pair.

records.chose: docs --check treats an absent README fence pair as NOT OWNED (green), while claude --check reds on absent markers
over: one uniform rule — red on missing markers for both owned blocks
silently skipping either way, with no output
records.because: docs runs in every consuming project, and a gate that fails on a file the project never opted into is a gate that gets switched off wholesale; claude is opt-in per invocation, so there a missing marker pair genuinely means the file failed to get wired up. The skip is not SILENT though — the write path prints the marker pair to paste, because a command that exits 0 having done nothing is the exact defect this harness exists to catch.

git checkout <ref> -- . to revert in place

records.chose: the difference was intended but undeclared for the one visible token, on top of a correspondence that was genuinely unmaintained — and the fix taken was the tier-1 one the discriminator names: derive, so the pair stops existing
records.because: Put side by side as instructed. The single token the detector saw (only in the dispatch: `resolve`) was NOT drift — it is a legitimate alias, and a banner listing it as a command of its own would be wrong. So candidate 3 won on that token: overlapping-but-deliberately-different domains that nobody had written down. But the correspondence itself had also genuinely drifted (banner 29 vs dispatch 30; v0.14.0's only merge conflict was two branches hand-editing the banner literal), so candidate 2 held for the pair's history. Both are now moot: src/commands.ts is the single declarative home, the banner is .map()ped from it, README's index is spliced from it, and aliases are a first-class field so `resolve` is dispatched without being advertised — the thing nobody had written down is now the thing that IS written down. Measured from an isolated worktree at b498b7d: redundancy goes 42 candidate pairs to 37, five removed and zero added, and this pair is gone from the pair set entirely rather than demoted below the floor. THE INSTRUMENT WAS NOT WRONG — the highest-prior candidate lost. redundancy reported this pair on every run since it shipped and was correct every time.

records.chose: derived the ENTIRE usage banner from the registry — grouped per-command lines with usage and summary — not just the <a|b|c> alternation the brief named
over: deriving only the alternation line and keeping the 25 hand-written curated help lines below it
records.because: the brief asked for the alternation literal to go away, and stopping there would have left 25 lines that name commands and drift silently. Those lines were also a CURATED SUBSET: they detailed the journal verbs and flags while omitting graph, overview, docs, claude, onboard, decompose, drift and phrasebook entirely, so the help screen was incomplete in exactly the way the README was. Deriving all 31 costs ~13 lines of banner and buys completeness. What was deliberately NOT absorbed: the per-command usage ERRORS (decide/conjecture/observed/dismiss print their own multi-paragraph help on bad input) — those stay hand-written, because a command's own error is the right place for its domain and its nuance, and the banner is an index.

records.chose: absorbed the README's pure one-liner command bullets into the registry's summary field, and kept every bullet carrying a WHY as authored detail below the fence
over: keeping all the authored bullets and letting the derived index duplicate the one-liners
deleting the whole ## Commands prose and generating the entire section
records.because: a bullet that only restates name-plus-one-line IS the list, not detail about it, so leaving it beside the derived index is the same two-spellings defect one level down — a reader seeing both and finding them different has no way to tell which is authoritative. Generating the whole section was rejected outright: most of that prose is argument no derivation can produce (judge is not notary, an advisory that fires every run is wallpaper, the measured reasoning for why because is uncapped) and it is why anyone adopts this instead of writing four vitest helpers. The rule applied: no WHY, absorb it (graph, overview, docs, claude, phrasebook); any WHY, keep it verbatim. The stray dismiss bullet moved INTO the journal sub-list where its six siblings live — that reader-facing defect was the finding, not just a symptom.

records.chose: the hook reads the parent session's cwd, not the subagent's working repo
records.because: Ran the discriminator. planetizer's journal — the parent session's cwd — reports exactly 5 OPEN CONJECTURE(S), and `cat .coherence/decisions/*.jsonl | grep -vc '"kind":"session"'` there returns exactly 74. Both of the hook's numbers match planetizer to the digit, so it is reading that repo's journal, not coherence's. Not a stale cache: the count was correct for the repo it was actually looking at, both times. Not an instrument defect either — stopReport calls the same readJournal + resolve that renderJournal calls, and computes correctly over whatever cwd it is handed. THE CONSEQUENCE IS A WORDING BUG, and it is the kind this project cares about: the message says OPEN CONJECTURE(S) IN THIS REPO, and for a subagent working in a different repo than its parent, 'this repo' names the wrong one — so the nag points at questions the agent cannot see and stays silent about the ones it just created. My own decisions went to coherence's journal correctly (npx coherence ran from the coherence directory), so only the REPORT crossed repos, never the writes.

records.chose: did not fix stopReport's 'in this repo' wording, which names the parent's cwd rather than the subagent's working repo
records.because: it is a real defect (d-a50185c8/d-9ed648e4 has the evidence) but it is outside the task I was given — the command registry — and a hook-message change alters what every agent in every consuming project reads at stop time. records.chose: derive the hookless session id as <branch>-<agent>-<YYYY-MM-DD>, and keep RANDOM ids for hook-minted sessions
over: keep newSessionId() as the fallback — one random file per hookless invocation
one shared journal file, no per-session split at all
<agent>-<date> without the branch
local calendar date instead of the UTC date
records.because: the branch MUST stay in the filename: distinct filenames are the entire reason two parallel branches never conflict on the journal, and that property is what the split-file layout was bought for. Dropping the branch would trade a merge conflict for a tidy PR. The date is taken from the record's own `at` (UTC) rather than a local clock so the filename and the timestamps inside it are on one clock; the cost is that an evening's work can straddle UTC midnight into two files, which month-grouped compaction absorbs completely. RESIDUAL COLLISION CASE, and it is safe: two agents both defaulting to agent "main" on one branch share one file. (a) Same branch means same checkout — git refuses to check one branch out in two worktrees, so genuinely concurrent agents have different branches by construction. (b) Even interleaved, appendFileSync is measured in this repo at 8 writers x 300 lines, 2400/2400 intact, 0 torn, and the same probe loses 1242/2400 with a seek-write writer, so it can see loss when loss exists. (c) The only thing actually lost is attribution between two agents that already declined to pass --agent. (d) The supported concurrency path — the SubagentStart hook — still mints random ids and is untouched.

records.chose: scope --compact's dirty refusal to .coherence/decisions/, and make an UNCOMMITTED (untracked) journal file a skip rather than a refusal
over: refuse whenever the whole working tree is dirty, as briefed
refuse on any untracked .jsonl too
records.because: the brief asked for a whole-tree refusal AND for a dogfood run on this repo, and this repo's tree is dirty by the requester's own hand (M src/hooks.ts, explicitly hands-off) — as literally stated the two requirements cannot both hold. The narrowing is also the correct scope on its merits: the loss --compact can cause is journal lines that git history does not hold, and an unrelated modified source file cannot be lost by moving journal lines. Untracked is a SKIP because an untracked .jsonl is exactly the live-session case (a session opened minutes ago, never committed) — refusing there makes the command unusable in any repo where an agent is running, which is every repo that needs it. What still REFUSES is the dangerous case: a TRACKED journal file whose content differs from HEAD, i.e. someone edited the record in place, which is the one thing this journal forbids and not something compaction should paper over.

records.chose: a 2-hour mtime quiet window, bounded from BOTH sides by measurement rather than picked
over: 24 hours
no window at all, relying only on the re-stat race guard
records.because: LOWER bound: it must exceed the gap between one agent's successive appends or compaction lands mid-session. Measured on this repo's own 14 session files: the largest gap between consecutive entries inside a single session is 14.1 min and the longest session spans 22.5 min, so 2h is ~8x the observed worst case. UPPER bound, and this is what kills 24h: the motivating case is ~20 files accumulated in ONE day and compacted before the PR goes up — a 24-hour window refuses exactly the work it was asked to tidy, which would make the feature useless on the day it is needed. The window is a heuristic so it is not the only guard: every source is re-stat'd immediately before its group is written and the group is abandoned whole if anything moved, and a fold that raced an append anyway DUPLICATES lines rather than losing them, which resolve()'s content-hash dedupe renders identically.

records.chose: make readJournal's sort TOTAL — (at, id, session) — so the render is a function of the record SET rather than of the file layout
over: leave the two-key sort and rely on the concatenation being timestamp-ordered
records.because: render-identity was only a coincidence before. The two-key sort left (at, id) ties to be settled by READ ORDER — directory listing, then line number — so the render was partly a function of which file a record sat in, which is precisely what compaction changes; resolve()'s last-write-wins dedupe would then render the other copy's agent/branch/commit. (at, id, session) can only tie for byte-identical duplicates, which dedupe to one entry anyway. Measured before changing it: 0 (at,id) ties and 0 duplicate ids across this repo's own 72 records, so it moved nothing on disk today and the before/after renders are identical. SIDE EFFECT WORTH NAMING: with the reader total, the ORDER of the concatenation can no longer reach the render, so the render-identity test is deliberately insensitive to it — the ordering property therefore needs its own direct assertion on file content, and it has one.

records.chose: the negative control the brief asked for — reversing the timestamp order of the concatenation — left the render-identity test GREEN, and only the separate file-content ordering assertion went red
records.because: a no-op test nobody has watched fail is indistinguishable from one that asserts nothing, and the first control failing to fire is exactly the shape of that failure
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes
the render-identity test asserts nothing
it is correct and insensitive by construction: readJournal's sort is total over (at, id, session), so line order inside a file cannot reach the render
records.discriminatedBy: a SECOND control that changes the record set rather than its order — disabling the unreadable-line guard so a garbage file gets folded with its bad line dropped. RAN IT: the render-identity test went red, losing exactly the line 'WARNING: 1 unreadable line(s) — skipped, not repaired.' So the test does assert, and the insensitivity to order is the second candidate, not the first.

records.chose: insensitive by construction, not vacuous — and the ordering property now has its own oracle
records.because: the second control RAN and the render-identity test went red on exactly one line: 'WARNING: 1 unreadable line(s) — skipped, not repaired.' vanished when the unreadable-line guard was disabled and a garbage file was folded with its bad line dropped. The test therefore asserts. The first control leaves it green because readJournal's sort is total over (at, id, session), so line order inside a file provably cannot reach the render — which is why the concatenation's ordering carries its own direct assertion on file content, and that assertion is what went red under the reversal (main-2026-06.jsonl is not in timestamp order).

couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes
compaction really did delete 10 files it should have kept
records.discriminatedBy: ls the directory and count — the subject is a directory, so ask the directory rather than the tally

records.chose: the instrument was wrong — the tally, not the compaction
records.because: ls said 5, and all 78 records rendered identically across nine shapes — nothing was lost. The REPORT was wrong: it derived after = plan.before - folded, which subtracted the 14 files unlinked and forgot the 4 written. Instrument, on the first candidate, again. Fixed by counting the directory instead of deriving the number (src/decisions.ts, compactJournal), and pinned by an assertion in the acceptance test that the reported 'N file(s) → M' matches readdir before and after — because the reported count is the number a human judges the run by, and it was the only thing in the whole feature that no test was reading.

records.chose: put --compact under `coherence decisions` rather than making it its own verb
over: a top-level `coherence compact`
records.because: the brief specified the flag, and it turns out to be the better home for a reason worth writing down: the entire contract of --compact is that it changes nothing `coherence decisions` prints, so the write living under the read it must not disturb puts the claim and its witness on the same line in the help text. It also costs no new dispatch entry, so commands.test.ts's dispatch-vs-registry totality oracle is untouched.

records.chose: batch reports resolve through execNamedTest in phrasebook.ts, the single shared executable arm
over: a separate batch code path in verify.ts alongside the per-claim one
teaching each of the three executable claim forms about batching individually
records.because: 'passes test', 'boundary … via test' and 'parity … via test' ALREADY funnel every runner invocation through execNamedTest. Intercepting there means the batch inherits all three forms — including the expensive boundary oracles — with one edit, and the fallback is literally the untouched body of the same function. Three call sites taught separately would be three chances to diverge on what green means.

records.chose: mirror -t by literal substring on the report's fullName field
over: regex-matching the claim name against fullName
exact equality against fullName
records.because: VERIFIED against vitest 4.1.10: -t is an UNANCHORED REGEX over fullName (ancestorTitles.join(' ')+' '+title). -t 'totality covers' matched 'write policy totality covers every op' — a substring spanning the describe/it boundary — and unescaped -t 'rejects unknown (a+b)' matched ZERO tests while the reEscape'd form matched one. Since the per-claim path always reEscapes first, an escaped-regex unanchored match IS exactly a literal substring test, so fullName.includes(name) is the precise mirror. Exact equality would silently red every claim anchored to a describe title rather than a full leaf name — the common case.

records.chose: support BOTH --outputFile and stdout, reading the file when the command carries --outputFile, and tolerating stdout via a brace-balanced scan for the last top-level object carrying testResults
over: stdout only with a whole-string JSON.parse
requiring --outputFile and erroring on a bare stdout command
records.because: MEASURED: a test doing process.stdout.write('RAW WRITE') put that text ahead of the report, and whole-file JSON.parse threw 'Unexpected token R'. vitest emits the report last, so the pollution observed was strictly BEFORE the JSON and a scan recovers it — but relying on that ordering for every consuming repo is a bet. --outputFile is immune (stdout dropped to 50 bytes, file parsed clean), so it is what the docs recommend; the stdout scan exists so the obvious ['npx','vitest','run','--reporter=json'] a reader will type first does not mysteriously fall back forever.

records.chose: green requires >=1 PASSED match and 0 failed, treating skipped matches as neither evidence nor failure
over: the literal brief wording 'every matching test passed', which would red a describe containing one it.skip
records.because: the mandate is to MIRROR the per-claim path, and mirroring beats the wording where they disagree. A describe with four its and one .skip: vitest -t <title> exits 0 with '4 passed | 1 skipped', testMatch '[1-9][0-9]* passed' matches, per-claim says GREEN. Requiring EVERY match to be passed would make batch STRICTER than the path it replaces and turn a config flip into a wave of new reds in repos that were honestly green. Requiring >=1 passed keeps the testMatch guarantee (positive evidence) without inventing a new one.

records.chose: record the batch marker RUN-level on VerifySection, not per-claim on ClaimRecord
over: a per-claim batched:true field alongside the verdict
no marker at all
records.because: checked mergeClaimRecords first, as instructed: its skip-doesn't-clobber branch does {...old}, so a per-claim marker would survive onto a verdict measured by the OTHER path in an earlier run — a provenance field that lies is worse than none. VerifySection is rewritten whole every run and takes part in no merge, so one field there is free of that hazard and reads correctly for scoped runs too. A verdict is a verdict; this sits next to commit/dirty as provenance about the instrument.

records.chose: treat only a non-running runner or an unparsable report as a batch crash; ignore the exit code entirely, and raise spawnSync maxBuffer to 64 MiB
over: treating a nonzero exit as a crash that triggers fallback
leaving maxBuffer at the spawnSync default
records.because: a suite with a red test exits nonzero, and that is exactly the run whose report is most worth reading — keying the fallback on exit status would fall back to the 30-minute path on every run that had a failure, i.e. precisely when you are iterating. The maxBuffer point is the same hazard by another route: the default is 1 MiB and a vitest JSON report embeds a full stack trace per failure, so the FAILING run is the one whose report arrives truncated and unparsable, which would have looked like a mysterious fallback that only ever happened when something was broken.

records.chose: add --from-report <file> as a third tier that reads a report an OUTER gate already produced
over: batch-only, where coherence always runs the suite itself
records.because: field data from a second consuming repo: their check.mjs already runs the whole suite, and coherence then ran it again — 17 targeted oracle runs at 4.51s each, of which '7 passed | 291 skipped' shows ~60s was pure import/transform cost for 298 tests to execute 7. Batch mode alone cuts 18 suite imports to 1; --from-report cuts it to ZERO, because the answer was already computed by the run that just finished. The flag is its own opt-in and needs no testBatch configured — the caller passing a path is asserting the file is current, which is a claim only the caller can make.

records.chose: name the zero-match verdict VANISHED ORACLE and treat three-state resolution as the feature, with speed as the side effect
over: reporting zero matches as a generic red
framing the whole feature as a performance optimization
records.because: the report distinguishes ran+passed, ran+failed, and DOES NOT EXIST. The per-claim path cannot see the third state — vitest -t exits 0 on a filter that matched nothing — so a renamed or deleted oracle reads as GREEN unless the project knew to configure testMatch. That is the same defect class as a typo'd claim verb: a hole plugged by a knob a reader has to know about. Batch mode observes absence directly, so testMatch has nothing left to do for a batched claim. A verdict named 'VANISHED ORACLE' says which of the three states it is; 'red' does not, and the distinction is the one that catches spec rot.

records.chose: keep the batch as shared EVIDENCE resolved per claim, never a shared verdict
over: one suite-level verdict applied to every executable claim
records.because: the per-claim path's best property is that each claim fails alone, naming its own oracle — that is what makes a red actionable instead of a summons to read the whole suite. Batching changes where the evidence comes from and nothing else: resolveFromBatch takes ONE name and returns ONE detail, so three claims over one report produce three independent verdicts (locked by a test asserting a green claim is not dragged down by two red neighbours sharing the report). Aggregating would have been simpler and would have been a regression.

records.chose: batching node:test consumers — no derivable format shipped in v0.17.0, so node:test is RECOGNIZED and refused with instructions rather than guessed at
records.because: measured on Node 25.2.1: node:test ships NO json reporter (node:test/reporters exports only default, dot, junit, lcov, spec, tap), so there is no report with a vitest-style concatenated fullName to read. Worse, its --test-name-pattern does NOT match a concatenated name — pattern 'outer group inner leaf' matched nothing while 'inner leaf' and 'outer group' each matched — so the vitest mirror (literal substring over fullName) would be WRONG for node:test, not merely unavailable. Parsing tap (nested sub-TAP) or junit (XML) is possible but the matching rule is a second semantic model, and shipping a mirror I have not verified is the one thing this feature is not allowed to do.

records.chose: node:test reports a PASSING entry named after the test FILE when --test-name-pattern matches nothing: pattern 'and +plus' over a file with no such test printed 'ok 1 - /tmp/nt-nested.test.ts', '# pass 1', and exited 0
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes

node:test treats the file-level subtest as the unit and marks it passed when it ran cleanly with zero matching descendants — so a vanished oracle is green AND a testMatch regex like '[1-9][0-9]* passed' is SATISFIED by it, making node:test consumers strictly more exposed to the vanished-oracle hole than vitest ones, where testMatch at least works
records.discriminatedBy: point a coherence 'passes test' claim at a name no node:test test has, with config.testMatch set to the README's recommended '[1-9][0-9]* passed', and see whether the claim goes green. If it does, the README's testMatch advice does not protect node:test projects at all and the batch path is the only real fix for them.

records.chose: the file-level-pass candidate — plus an independent arg-order defect that defeats testMatch even harder
records.because: ran the discriminating test on Node 25.2.1 with config.testMatch set to the README's recommended '[1-9][0-9]* passed'. BOTH routes make a vanished oracle green: (1) with the pattern as a real node option, a pattern matching nothing still reports the FILE as one passing test ('ok 1 - <file>', '# pass 1', exit 0) — the conjectured candidate, confirmed; (2) and there is a second, worse route nobody would notice — node stops parsing its own options at the first positional, so a config.test of [node, --test, <glob>, --test-name-pattern] passes the flag to the SCRIPT, the filter is silently inert, the WHOLE suite runs and passes, and every claim goes green regardless of what it names. Either way testMatch is satisfied, so the README's advice does not protect node:test projects.

records.chose: make batch the DEFAULT full-tier path (deriving the command from config.test for vitest) and put the serial per-claim profile behind an explicit --serial-oracles / oracleExecution:"serial", refusing loudly when neither is available
over: the additive design shipped an hour earlier: feature OFF unless testBatch is configured, per coherence's own 'no behaviour change by default' discipline
keeping serial as the fallback default and merely documenting the cost
records.because: the additive design is right for a FEATURE and wrong for a DEFECT. 20-35 minutes to re-derive evidence one boot already contains is not a conservative default, it is a bad one nobody chose — and the measured second repo shows consumers do not discover the knob: they were paying the suite's import cost 18 times WHILE their own check.mjs paid it once. An opt-in fast path means the projects that most need it are the least likely to have it. Fail-closed is the harness's own doctrine applied to itself: a consumer must TYPE --serial-oracles to get the expensive profile, and an unknown runner refuses with three named ways out rather than silently choosing the worst one.

records.chose: prove the report file postdates the batch run (mtime vs a pre-spawn timestamp) and refuse a leftover one as stale
over: reading whatever is at the --outputFile path, as the first implementation did
records.because: found while chasing a suspiciously fast smoke run: if the runner exits WITHOUT writing (a config error, a collection failure) and a report from a previous run is still on disk, reading it resolves every claim from evidence about code that no longer exists — and it looks completely healthy. That is strictly worse than a crash, which at least falls back loudly. A pre-spawn timestamp plus statSync makes it structural. 2s of slack absorbs coarse filesystem mtime granularity and cannot admit a previous run's file.

records.chose: the shared EVOLUTION store (src/evolution.ts) is an IN-PROCESS MEMO keyed <root>|<limit>, and persists nothing
over: a status.json evolution/churn section written by every history-reading command
a committed churn artifact under outputDir keyed by HEAD
leaving the derivation spelled three times (decompose, drift, scene) and only documenting the duplication
records.because: the finding was REDUNDANCY, not latency: one git derivation spelled three times, with the BULK band and a bare 200-commit window free to drift apart. A persisted cache fixes the wrong problem and adds a new one — it would be rewritten by every command that touches history and land in every diff a reader has to review, so the repo pays perpetual diff noise for a git call the CLI makes a handful of times per process. The memo is valid because the CLI is one command per process and HEAD cannot move underneath it; _resetEvolutionMemo() exists so a test process, the one place that assumption is false, can drop it.

records.chose: the command is named `mass` and there is no umbrella verb over it
over: `energy` — an assembler command that would run mass + drift + churn and print one composite score
folding the mass dimensions into `decompose` or `drift` as extra sections
records.because: MASS is the thing actually measured: lines, files, symbols, dependency counts, and whatever the project's own measures probe. It is a scalar the ratchet can pin, and every dimension is addressable by key — which is what makes a baseline, a tolerance and a --raise subject possible. `energy` would name a composite nobody can point at: a score assembled from a snapshot plus a derivative has no unit, no baseline that means anything, and no key to hang a tolerance on. An umbrella command would also make the failure ambiguous — a reader could not tell which instrument said no.

records.chose: a mass excursion becomes a journal entry ONLY under --raise, as a Finding fed through raiseFindings
over: calling `observed` implicitly for every dimension on every run, so mass fed the tracked-metric machinery automatically
writing a conjecture directly from mass.ts, bypassing the cap and the dedupe
records.because: `observed` is for a metric whose owner has already declared a BAND — value, baseline, threshold — so 'outside' means something the harness did not invent. Mass has no band: the baseline is a PIN, and a pin plus a tolerance of zero would make every ordinary growth run an implicit journal write on a read-only report. That is precisely the surprising-write failure raise.ts's header says kills a mechanism wholesale. Going through raiseFindings also buys the two things a hand-rolled write loses: the per-run cap spent round-robin across advisories, and dedupe on a subject that carries no magnitude — so a second run after another 400 lines does not mint a second question about lines|total.

records.chose: the mass ratchet's growth failure PRESCRIBES `coherence decide` — it says the movement gained parts nobody named, then names the two commands that settle it
over: printing a silent numeric diff (lines|total 4 → 9) and letting the reader decide what to do
failing with a generic 'threshold exceeded' and a link to the config key
records.because: a numeric diff tells the reader what `git diff --stat` already told them and settles nothing. The ratchet cannot know whether 460 new lines bought a feature or an accident, and the only party who can say is the one who wrote them — this run, while they still remember, not a reader six months out. So the gate does not ask for justification, it asks for a RECORD and then a re-pin: `coherence decide "<what the new mass buys>"` followed by `--update-baseline`. That also makes the re-pin honest — the baseline moves with an entry beside it saying why, instead of moving because somebody wanted the build green.

records.chose: a per-component mass key falls back to the DIR (`lines|.`) when no component node carries a label, never to the raw graph id (`lines|c:.`)
over: decompose's componentMap fallback (`compLabel.get(parent) ?? parent`), which yields the raw `c:<dir>` id
records.because: the first dogfood run of `coherence mass` on this repo — which declares no components — printed `lines|c:.`, and that key would then have been written into mass-baseline.json, quoted in --check failures and used as a --raise subject for the life of the project. A baseline key is an ADDRESS somebody types; a graph-internal id escaping into it is the kind of leak that is impossible to rename later because it is in everyone's committed baseline. decompose's fallback is fine where it lives (an in-memory grouping label nobody stores).

records.chose: the harness's own last 400 commits show a NET +22,898 LOC, but `mass` measures the tree at 19,898 lines — the history added more than the repo currently holds, over a window that does not obviously reach the repo's first commit
couldBe: the two instruments count different FILE SETS: git counts every tracked file (README.md at 111KB, RELEASE-NOTES.md, the .coherence journal, public/ artifacts when they were tracked), while mass counts only the 76 nodes in the derived graph (src + test .ts)
the window is not the whole history: 400 commits may reach back past a large deletion, so net-over-window and current-size are simply not comparable quantities
churn: rewrites delete and re-add the same region, and --shortstat counts both sides, so net can exceed final size wherever a file was rewritten rather than appended to
records.discriminatedBy: run `git log --shortstat` over the SAME 400 commits restricted to the graph's own paths (`-- src test`) and compare the net to lines|total; then repeat with no -n limit. If the path-restricted net lands near 19,898 the file-set explanation wins; if only the unlimited range does, the window explanation wins; if neither closes the gap, it is churn and the two numbers were never comparable.

records.chose: the two instruments count different FILE SETS
records.because: Ran the discriminating test. (1) The WINDOW candidate is dead outright: `git rev-list --count HEAD` is 80, so the 400-commit window already spans the entire history — net(400) and net(all) are the same number, 22,898. (2) Scoping the same all-history --shortstat to the graph's own paths (`-- src test`) gives net +18,995 against a measured lines|total of 19,898, and the residual is accounted for by the four files this change added being present in the graph and absent from any commit. The 3,903-line gap is README.md (111KB), RELEASE-NOTES.md and the .coherence journal — tracked by git, invisible to the graph walk. (3) Churn is therefore at most a minor term, not the explanation. Consequence: the report now NAMES the universe on the spark line ('ALL tracked files, not just the graph's'), because printing two numbers from two different file sets in one report is how a reader ends up distrusting the wrong instrument.

records.chose: claim HOLDING COST is a RUN-LEVEL vector on VerifySection (cost: {totalMs, claims[]}), rewritten whole every run
over: a per-claim ms field on ClaimRecord, alongside the verdict it describes
records.because: the argument the 'batched' field already settled applies verbatim: mergeClaimRecords' skip-carry branch keeps a PREVIOUS run's verdict when this run only skipped a claim (--fast skipping the executable tier is the common case), so a per-claim ms would ride through that branch and start describing a run that did not happen. A verdict is a verdict; a timing is provenance about the instrument, like commit/dirty. The property is asserted directly in test/verify.test.ts ('REWRITTEN WHOLE: a dropped claim leaves no ghost row').

records.chose: cost prefers the RUNNER's own per-assertion duration over verify's wall clock, and records WHICH clock answered (msSource: report|wall)
over: wall time around evalClaim for every claim, uniformly
report time only, leaving non-executable claims uncosted
records.because: on a batch-resolved claim the wall clock times a MAP LOOKUP — the suite already ran once, lazily, and whichever claim happened to trigger it would be charged the whole spawn while the rest read as free. The runner's duration is the only reading that attributes cost to the claim that caused it. Wall time is still the honest (and only) reading for a typecheck, a fetch or a serial runner boot, so both survive — but never blended: a mixed column with no provenance is unreadable, so the source rides per row into status.json.

records.chose: crossing HEAT is the MAX over the chokepoint's defining files of that file's churn share, and ABSENT (no entry) when unmeasurable
over: the SUM of the defining files' shares
the MEAN over the defining files
zero-filling a symbol with no graph node or no history
records.because: a symbol can resolve to more than one file (an overload, a re-export, the same name in two places). Summing lets cold twins push a crossing past a share it never had; averaging lets a cold twin HIDE a genuinely hot definition — the failure that matters, since the question heat answers is 'is anyone working near this chokepoint' and one hot definition is a yes. Zero-fill is the same lie the batch report's absent durations would tell: an unmeasurable temperature rendered as cold is a claim nobody measured, so a missing symbol or an empty history yields no entry and the render says '—'. A symbol IN the graph over a real history that was simply never touched is a measured 0, which is a different fact and is kept.

records.chose: holding-cost findings rank LAST in verify's raise order, behind never-red, warned-kind and refutation
over: interleaving cost with the correctness advisories by severity
records.because: cost is the weakest signal the harness produces: an expensive claim can be entirely correct, and often the honest answer is that the domain really is that big. The three advisories above it ask whether the RECORD is trustworthy; cost asks about the APPARATUS. Since the raise cap is per run and spent round-robin, the caller's order decides who goes first within a round — putting cost last is what guarantees 'expensive to keep true' never displaces a question about whether something is true at all. Pinned by test/verify.test.ts under a cap of 1.

records.chose: status.json stores only the TOP-5 of the cost ranking (COST_RECORD_CAP), not every claim's timing
over: a full per-claim timing vector in the record
records.because: the record exists to be READ — the panel shows the head of it, a jq one-liner wants the expensive tail named. A row per claim would grow status.json by the size of the whole claim set every run to carry a tail nothing displays, and status.json is a tracked file whose diff a human reviews. The console report and the record are both slices of ONE ordering, so the panel can never disagree with the console about what is expensive.

records.chose: the panel's masthead height became a derived function (mastheadHeight) shared by the renderer and the interactive scroll math
over: leaving the keypress handler's hard-coded '- 3' and letting the energy strip make it wrong by a row
records.because: the strip is conditional, so the masthead is now 3 rows or 4. renderFrame already derived body height from head.length, but the cursor-visibility math in the keypress loop hard-coded 3 — with the strip present the window and the cursor would have disagreed by one row, which reads as a scrolling bug nobody can reproduce without a cost record. One function, two callers, no arithmetic to keep in sync.

records.chose: the atlas render normalizes its heat bar across the crossings on the map, while the RECORD stores the raw 0..1 share
over: storing the rendered glyph, or normalizing against an absolute scale
records.because: a bar is a comparison and the useful comparison is 'which crossing on THIS map is hot' — against an absolute scale every crossing in a calm repo renders as one glyph and the map says nothing. But normalization is a rendering decision, and the panel normalizes over its own top-8 instead, so the stored value has to be the measurement: raw share in, each consumer scales it.

records.chose: vitest's per-assertion duration may measure IN-WORKER time rather than a share of the pooled run's wall clock, so sum(claims.ms) can exceed or undershoot the suite's actual wall time
couldBe: the durations are honest per-test in-worker measurements, and a worker POOL runs several files concurrently — so the sum counts the same wall seconds once per worker and overshoots by roughly the parallelism
the durations exclude per-file import/collection cost, which on a real suite dominates, so the sum UNDERshoots the wall clock instead
records.discriminatedBy: run a real vitest suite of N files that each sleep a known amount, time the batch spawn with a wall clock, and compare that measurement against sum(assertion durations) from the same run's JSON report

records.chose: in-worker per-test time under a concurrent pool: sum(claims.ms) overshoots suite wall time by roughly the pool parallelism
records.because: RAN THE DISCRIMINATION. A purpose-built vitest 4.1.9 project: 4 test files, one test each, every test sleeping 800ms, run through the same batch command coherence issues (vitest run --reporter=json --outputFile). Measured wall time of the batch spawn: 1.04s. sum(assertion durations) from that same run's report: 3207.7ms — a 3.1x OVERSHOOT, and the report's own per-file startTime values are identical to the millisecond (1785465173847-849), i.e. all four files ran concurrently in the pool. Each duration is a truthful ~800ms in-worker reading; they simply count the same wall seconds once per worker. The instrument is NOT wrong — the durations are real — but they are per-test costs, not shares of a wall clock, and they must never be presented as 'the suite takes this long'. What ships is consistent with that: the report says 'to verify N claim(s) ... per run' and the per-claim rows carry their source, so the number is read as summed per-claim cost. Undershoot (import/collection cost excluded) was NOT observed here, but this suite has trivial imports, so it stays plausible for an import-heavy suite; the overshoot candidate is the one this test settles.

records.chose: could not dogfood either new instrument on the coherence repo itself
records.because: coherence carries no *.spec.md and no coherence.config.json of its own, so 'verify --fast' here reports 'claims: 0' (an empty cost vector, correctly below the floor and silent) and 'atlas' reports 'no atlas config — nothing to render'. Both features were instead exercised on a purpose-built vitest project with real git history, which is also what discriminated the duration conjecture: cost printed 3.2s over 5 claims with four 800ms report-sourced rows and one 2ms wall-sourced typecheck; atlas printed 'heat █ 75%' for two crossings defined in a file touched by 3 of 4 considered commits, and the panel drew 'energy  cost 3.2s · top 804ms Dogfood  |  heat ██ mintToken 75%'.

records.chose: the cost report says '<n>s across N claim(s) — summed per-claim cost … (a pooled runner overlaps some of it)' rather than '<n>s to verify N claims'
over: the shorter 'to verify N claim(s)' wording the first cut shipped
records.because: the discrimination run for d-fe9ebf1e (resolved) measured a 3.1x gap between the sum of per-assertion durations and the batch spawn's wall clock, because a worker pool counts the same wall seconds once per worker. The first wording reads as 'the tier took this long', which is a claim the instrument cannot support. The number is honest as a SUM OF PER-CLAIM COSTS and is what a ranking needs; the sentence now says exactly that, and the test asserts the qualifier so it cannot be shortened back by accident.

records.chose: atlas heat rebases commit paths at the CALLER via shared gitPrefix()/rebaseCommits() in evolution.ts (componentMap now uses the same spelling)
over: teaching crossingHeat about Config (it stays a pure function of graph+commits)
normalizing paths inside readCommitLog itself (componentMap already strips the prefix, so log-level normalization would double-strip for every existing consumer)
records.because: the consumer running with cfg.root=app/ measured heat 0% on every crossing — git speaks repo-root paths, the graph speaks cfg.root paths, and the translation existed but was spelled privately inside componentMap where the next consumer (atlas heat) could not find it; lifting it to the evolution store is the same one-spelling fix the store itself was

records.chose: the README frames coherence as an inference-economy machine: the price ladder (inferred > read > unaskable), claims/nonTransition/--over as cached inference, the tier system AS the ladder, and the reducer dissolve > declare > infer
over: keeping the spec+verification framing as the lead — it describes the mechanism and leaves the purpose to be inferred, which is the exact cost the doctrine names
a separate DOCTRINE.md — a frame nobody routes to is a frame nobody holds; in-README it meets every reader before the first command
records.because: the harness's own commands only cohere under this frame: atlas nonTransition is cached NEGATIVE inference, --over is a cached search, and tier-3/2/1 are literally the three prices

records.chose: the doctrine section carries both faces — economy and trust — in one section, closing on the panel image
over: a separate trust section following the economy one
opening with trust and deriving economy from it
records.because: they are one quantity from two observers (builder: what does this cost; relier: what may I assume), and splitting them invites a reader to pick a favorite and read half the doctrine

records.chose: the price ladder precedes the enforcement ladder, which keeps its heading and gains one bridging clause
over: retitling or replacing 'The mental model: the enforcement ladder'
folding the enforcement tiers into the new section
records.because: the tier vocabulary is load-bearing in src/panel.ts, scene-model.ts and a dozen README back-references ('tier-1 on the ladder above'); the frame is new, the tier names are not

records.chose: the envelope image closes the doctrine as its unifying assembly — a third subsection after economy and trust, with the journal named as signal residue
over: restructuring the whole section around the envelope as the lead image
leaving the envelope for the v0.20.0 release notes only
records.because: the envelope CONTAINS the panel (a panel is one envelope component) and synthesizes both faces — penetrations are where anchoring effort concentrates, continuity is why totality oracles exist (a totality oracle is a blower-door test), and the constant-motion point gives the journal its mechanism: maintenance signal must be exhaust of the work itself because the crew is the weather; restructuring would have re-litigated a section committed hours earlier, and release-notes-only would leave the best frame off the page readers actually route to

records.chose: economy reads a 400-commit window (HIST = 400), sharing drift's and mass's memoized git log
over: 200, atlas heat's churn window
2000, decompose's all-time archaeology window
records.because: closure is a TRAJECTORY instrument like drift and mass, not an all-time grade: 400 gives ~50 concern-commits per trend bucket, and reusing the same <root>|400 key means the whole run costs one git read in-process.

records.chose: the closure universe is the graph's file nodes, with spec context = the owning components' spec files at their real line counts
over: counting a component's CLAIMS instead of its spec lines
dropping spec context entirely and measuring code only
records.because: a reader loading a change loads the spec that governs it; claims undercount the prose a reader actually reads. Touched files outside the graph (docs, config, lockfiles) are dropped and the caption NAMES that universe — mass.ts:250-258's precedent: a number whose universe is not the table's must say so on the line.

records.chose: closure LINE counts come from the CURRENT tree via fileStats, an approximation named in the report caption
over: a per-commit `git show` to get each file's size at that commit
records.because: the advisory ranks closures against each other over a recent window; per-commit precision costs a git read per file per commit on every run to move numbers the judgement does not turn on. An approximation that says it is one is honest; an expensive exact number nobody asked for is not.

records.chose: a moved sink is re-addressed by MATCHED DISAPPEARANCE: an unmatched site inherits a baselined review only if a site with the same context|expr vanished, one for one

The ratchet's whole value is site-level, so this buys quiet at the price of the thing it protects

git-rename-aware reconciliation (--find-renames / log --follow) — most precise, but it makes a tree-reading ratchet depend on VCS history: shallow CI clones, non-git consumers, and uncommitted working-tree moves (exactly when CI runs --check) all break it, and it still misses a move done as copy-then-delete
basename-only or path-normalized keys — still breaks on a rename and collides across same-named files (index.ts everywhere); strictly worse than either real option
keep failing on a move but with a friendlier message — the incident is that the alarm was DISBELIEVED, and a better-worded false alarm is still a false alarm
records.because: a ratchet baseline is a cached review, and a cached fact that expires on a rename is premise rot one layer down. Keying by path made a refactor manufacture false security alarms in proportion to how much code it moved (hoist: 4 of 7 reported 'new' sites were untouched). Conservation of count per context|expr is what keeps the loosening honest — relocation changes WHERE a reviewed site lives, duplication changes HOW MUCH unreviewed surface exists, and only the second is news

records.chose: the false-negative the fix ACCEPTS: a sink that moved into a genuinely more exposed file no longer fails --check; it is reported by name, from → to, instead
over: gating on the move as well (fail --check on any relocation) — that is the status quo and the reason the ratchet got disbelieved
gating only on moves that cross a component boundary — needs a notion of 'more exposed' the sinks lint does not have, and would fire on every extraction refactor, which is the exact case that broke
records.because: the sink CONTEXT (sql-ident vs html-value) is still part of the address, so a move that changes the KIND of sink is novel and does fail. What is given up is path-level exposure judgment, which the lint never actually had — it only ever knew that a path string changed. Moving the fact from silent to READ (an explicit MOVED block with old → new) is the honest rung on the price ladder for something the tool cannot decide

records.chose: when several byte-identical sites share one context|expr, WHICH new path inherits which vanished review is arbitrary — a test that asserted the moved site by path passed only by walk order (render.ts sorting before tools.ts), and flipped when a third file was added
couldBe: the instrument is wrong — the thing that PRODUCED this number, not the thing it describes
the pairing is genuinely under-determined and only the COUNT is a real guarantee — attribution is cosmetic and the report's from → to line can name the wrong 'from' when duplicates exist
a nearest-path heuristic (longest shared directory prefix) would recover the intended pairing in nearly every real refactor, making the reported from → to trustworthy rather than merely deterministic
records.discriminatedBy: replay hoist's actual eight-subsystem extraction through reconcile and check whether any context|expr had >1 vanished site; if none did, the ambiguity never fires in practice and the heuristic buys nothing. records.chose: left conventions.ts unchanged — its baseline is name-keyed and is already move-immune
over: applying the same matched-disappearance reconciliation to the conventions ratchet for symmetry
records.because: measured it, did not assume: baselined a guard at 2 call sites, then moved BOTH its declaration and a call site into a new subsystem dir. Ratchet stayed green. The key is {name, sites} and callSites() counts matches across the whole source set regardless of which file they live in, so relocation is invisible to it by construction. Its real sensitivity is fan-out GROWTH, which is signal, not noise — an extraction that genuinely adds call sites should fire. Symmetry is not a reason to add machinery to a component that does not have the defect

records.chose: the ambiguous case exists but did not arise; conservation holds and attribution stayed unforced
records.because: Replayed hoist's real extraction against the pre-refactor baseline, which is the discriminating test the conjecture named. Two context|expr keys DID carry multiple baselined sites — sql-ident|frame.reference.label at (patient.ts, shared/paths/divergence.ts) and sql-ident|u.characteristic at (patient.ts, shared/paths/schemas.ts) — so the ambiguous case is real, not hypothetical. But in both, exactly ONE site vanished (the patient.ts copy the extraction moved) while the sibling stayed live, so each new address absorbed exactly one vanished entry and attribution was never contested. The run reconciled 7 flagged sites into 4 MOVED and 3 genuinely novel, which is the correct split. Conclusion: ambiguity requires >1 vanished site sharing a key, which this refactor never produced — the count-conserving design is right and the tests are right to assert the count rather than the attribution

records.chose: a baseline cannot be CONSTRUCTED without declaring its rename semantics — the omission becomes a compile error, not a default
over: a shared reconcile() implementation across the three ratchets, which would paper over a real semantic difference: sink sites are DISCOVERED so a move should be forgiven, while components are DECLARED so a rename arguably SHOULD be signal
leaving each ratchet to answer independently, which is how we got three schemes and three different answers with nothing forcing the third author to notice there was a question
supplying a safe default (forgive moves everywhere), which trades a loud wrong answer for a quiet one
records.because: sidecar.ts already owns baseline I/O (readBaseline/writeBaseline) but nothing owns baseline IDENTITY — what counts as the same pinned fact across time. So the question got answered three times, differently, by three authors who never had to notice they were answering it: lint-sinks keyed kind|file|expr (broke on every refactor until v0.20.1), conventions keyed {name,sites} (immune by construction, verified by experiment), mass keys lines|<component> (a rename still reads as vanish+new). Shipping the lint-sinks fix DEEPENED the asymmetry — one ratchet now understands moves and the others do not. The fix is a shared OBLIGATION, not a shared implementation: a baseline type parameterized by an explicit rename policy — forgives-moves | immune-by-key | rename-is-signal — so all three answers stay legal and the omission stops being one. That is the harness's own dissolve>declare>infer applied to itself: today the policy is inferred from whatever the author happened to write; this makes it declared at the type, and the missing declaration unrepresentable

records.chose: Treat coherence's three tier-3 red crossings as NOT security concerns under the actual deployment, and record that the atlas security flag is over-applied here rather than acting on the alarm

records.because: Measured: 14 of 18 crossings carry security:true, so the flag fires on 78% of the graph and distinguishes almost nothing — it reads as 'this is a crossing', not 'this is a risk'. Taken individually under the real deployment, a CLI an owner runs in their own tree: loadConfig (project-source -> shell) is the only genuine execution surface, and it is exactly the trust level of npm test running package.json scripts — if you run the tool in a tree you already execute that tree's code, so it adds no exposure. buildGraph reads repo text into a model and executes nothing; its real failure mode is VACUITY, already governed by the non-vacuity floor, which is a correctness gate not a security one. readJsonOrRefuse reads the tool's own status.json and baselines, where the risk is corruption rather than attack, and v0.24.0 already fixed that by separating absent from unreadable. The threat model in which all three become real is pointing coherence at a repo you do NOT trust — an unfamiliar PR, a dependency under evaluation, an agent cloning something arbitrary. That has ZERO instances across three adopters, all owned by the same person. So the red is technically accurate (tier-3, no boundary claim, on a security-flagged crossing) and the ALARM is not. DISCRIMINATOR, so this can go stale honestly: if coherence is ever run against a tree its operator did not write, re-open this — loadConfig becomes arbitrary code execution from untrusted config and earns a boundary claim immediately. Until then, writing three claims to clear a red would be manufacturing evidence for a threat with no instances

events.canonical:
DECISION JOURNAL — this repo keeps one, and you are expected to write to it.

When you make a decision — a point where the work could have gone more than one
way and you picked — record it BEFORE moving on:

  coherence decide "<what you chose>" --over "<what you rejected>" --because "<why>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"

YOUR SESSION ID IS {{session}}. Pass it on every call — it is what keeps your
decisions attributable to you when four other agents are writing at the same time.

SWARM GYROSCOPE — read the durable field before acting:
  coherence orient
  coherence work inspect

`orient` selects one heading from strict evidence; it does not grant authority.
Only an orchestrator or explicitly authorized coordinator creates or hands off work.
Freeze objective, observable success, risk, authority, owner, dependencies, and scope
before dispatch; add parent/dependency/read/write flags when the boundary grants them:
  coherence work create "OBJECTIVE" --success "OBSERVABLE_RESULT" --risk high \
    --authority orchestrator-delegated --granted-by "ORCHESTRATOR" \
    --boundary "GRANTED_SCOPE" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"
Owners advance only the exact assignment printed by SessionStart. Re-inspect after
each mutation because predecessor tokens deliberately expire instead of last-writer-win.
Navigate explicit provenance with: coherence consequence inspect "work:WORK_ID"

`--over` is repeatable and it is the field that matters most: what you REJECTED is
what stops the next agent re-litigating a settled question. If you rejected nothing,
omit it — an unexamined choice and a forced one should not look alike.

WHEN A NUMBER SURPRISES YOU, DOUBT THE INSTRUMENT BEFORE THE SUBJECT — and record
the question even if you cannot chase it. An unresolved conjecture is a real entry:

  coherence conjecture "<the surprising observation>" --could-be "<explanation>" \
    --discriminated-by "<the test that would separate them>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"
  coherence resolved <id> --because "<what that test showed>" --as "<which candidate won>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"
  coherence dismiss <id> --because "<why it is not worth chasing>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"

You need not supply "the instrument is wrong" — it is added for you. It is the
highest-prior explanation for a surprising measurement and the one everyone skips.

WHEN YOU OBSERVE A DEFECT, RECORD IT BEFORE THE REPAIR ERASES THE EVIDENCE:

  coherence defect "<what failed>" --evidence "<the reproducer, output, or field report>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"

This is your assessed conclusion, not machine proof. If whether it is a defect is
still an open question, use conjecture instead. Attach each affected path with --file.
Redact credentials, tokens, personal data, and customer data: this record is committed.

`dismiss` is NOT `resolved`. Use it when the question is real and nobody intends to
answer it — it renders in its own section, saying exactly that, and it stops the
advisories re-raising the same finding. Answering something you did not answer is the
one thing this journal cannot recover from.

BEFORE YOU ADD A CONCEPT, COUNT ITS INSTANCES. A mechanism with no subjects in this
project is a FINDING, not a feature — and the finding is usually a subtraction that
does the same work. Record what you measured, what you would have built, and the
QUERY that decided it, because the answer is a function of the project and will change:

  coherence decide "not X — measured N instances" --over "<the mechanism you did not build>" \
    --because "<the query, so the next agent can re-run it instead of re-arguing>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"

WHEN YOU FIX A BUG, DECIDE WHAT HAPPENS TO ITS CLASS — dissolve > declare > infer.
Best: make the class UNREPRESENTABLE — remove the duplicated state, narrow the type,
collapse the second spelling of the domain that let two copies disagree. Next: PIN it —
an invariant anchored by a boundary whose guard goes red if the class returns, plus a
`## refutations` line recording what you actually observed broken; a fixed bug is a
measured negative control, and it is evidence only if it is written down. A spot fix
is the floor, not the fix — if the stronger rungs were out of reach, say why:

  coherence decide "spot-fixed <bug>; class survives" --over "dissolving <the state that allows it>" \
    --because "<why unrepresentable/pinned was not reachable today>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"

WHEN YOU FORM A MULTI-STEP PLAN, MAKE ITS PREDICTION FALSIFIABLE before acting:
  coherence experiment create "<what you expect will work>" --context "<file you expect to need>" \
    --action "<planned action>" --success "<observable success criterion>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"
The command prints stable action/criterion ids and a close template. Closing derives
success, failure, or inconclusive from evidence for EVERY id; a Stop or a checked box
never becomes success by itself.

Two more verbs:
  coherence blocked "<what you could not do>" --because "<why>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"
  coherence retract <id> --because "<what refuted it>" --session "{{session}}" --agent "{{agent}}"

This gates nothing. It cannot fail your build and it is not a checklist — log the
handful of choices a reader who never saw your transcript would need, not every step.
A job that logs three real decisions is worth more than one that logs thirty steps.
